- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or mixed, model often underestimates; adjust downward bias, especially if recent history shows volatility.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct — apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast growth by 10–20% for 3–5 days post-spike.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of price decline after peak), model often fails to recognize it — add a “reversion buffer” to forecast, especially if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to be overly optimistic in early periods (e.g., first 5–7 days) — apply a “lag correction”: reduce initial forecast by 5–10% if sentiment is weak or mixed.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “bullish” signals (e.g., 3+ consecutive 1.00 values), model often overcorrects — apply a “sentiment dampener”: reduce forecast by 5–15% if sentiment is high and price is rising.
